---
title: "Fit multiple fisheries and surveys"
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tinyAM)
source_files <- list.files(system.file("R", package = "tinyAM"),
  pattern = "[.](R|rdb|rdx)$", full.names = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", warning = TRUE,
  cache.extra = list(package = as.character(packageVersion("tinyAM")),
    R = as.character(getRversion()), RTMB = as.character(packageVersion("RTMB")),
    mgcv = as.character(packageVersion("mgcv")),
    sources = unname(tools::md5sum(source_files)),
    inputs = sim_cod_obs))
```

Different fishing gears remove different parts of a shared population. Surveys
also differ in coverage and selectivity. tinyAM represents these differences
with fleet-specific fishing mortality and survey-specific catchability, while
retaining one population and natural-mortality surface.

Here we use a simulated cod population inspired by 3Ps: active trawl, longline
and gillnet fisheries, an offshore RV-like survey, and a coastal
Sentinel-gillnet-like survey. These are teaching data, not observations from the
3Ps assessment. No SimSurvey installation is needed to use them. The
[dataset help](../reference/sim_cod_obs.html) documents generation, monitoring
assumptions and the separate truth object.

## Inspect the input keys

```{r inputs}
dat <- sim_cod_obs
check_tam_data(dat)
head(dat$catch)
head(dat$index)
```

Catch has a complete year–age grid within each `fleet`. An unavailable catch is
`NA`; it does not imply a closure. Each index row identifies `survey` and
`samp_time`. Both simulated surveys observe the same annual snapshot, so their
sampling fraction is zero. This deliberately removes seasonal timing from the
example.

F covariates belong in catch, q covariates in index, and recruitment/N/M
covariates in the optional population table. The same routing applies to a
single-fleet assessment. Fleet labels alone do not allocate an aggregate catch
among fisheries: separate observed catches are required.

The RV-like survey covers a broad offshore footprint. The regional survey
concentrates denser sampling in a northern coastal band and has dome-shaped
selection. The simulated coastline and depth restrictions are approximations.
The Sentinel-like program retains swept-area sampling; it does not reproduce
net saturation or literal fish-per-net CPUE.

```{r footprints, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Survey footprints on the synthetic grid. The northern edge represents the coast; grey cells are outside each survey's footprint."}
local({
  old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.8, 2.2, 0.8),
             mgp = c(2.8, 0.8, 0), cex = 0.85)
  on.exit(par(old))
  grid <- sim_cod_truth$footprint
  for (survey in c("RV", "Sentinel")) {
    selected <- grid[[survey]]
    plot(grid$x, grid$y, asp = 1, pch = 15, cex = 0.45,
      col = "grey90", xlab = "East-west (km)", ylab = "North-south (km)",
      main = if (survey == "RV") "RV-like" else "Sentinel-gillnet-like")
    points(grid$x[selected], grid$y[selected], pch = 15, cex = 0.45,
    col = tam_cols()[if (survey == "RV") 1 else 7])
  }
})
```

Catch inputs are expanded monitoring estimates, not the simulator's true
catches or raw counts of aged fish. Keep these distinctions when preparing your
own data. Genuine zeros remain in the inputs but are excluded from the current
lognormal likelihood. Missing biological samples must not be converted to zero
catches.

## Describe each fleet within one formula

Start with fleet-specific annual effects and selectivity shapes. `for_fleet()`
evaluates its inner formula only on the named fleet. Each inner formula includes
an intercept, so the outer formula uses `~ 0 +` to avoid an extra common baseline.

```{r fleet-formula, cache=TRUE}
fishing <- ~ 0 +
  for_fleet("Trawl", ~ factor(year) + logistic(age)) +
  for_fleet("Longline", ~ factor(year) + logistic(age)) +
  for_fleet("Gillnet", ~ factor(year) + double_logistic(age))
```

The trawl and longline relationships ascend toward a plateau; the gillnet curve
can decline at older ages. These age-based shapes are hypotheses about the
observed catches. The generator selects fish by length, and variability in
length at age means its average age relationship need not match these curves
exactly.
The plotted curves are gear-selection inputs; realized F also reflects spatial
access, capture and local depletion.

```{r selection, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Generating selectivity curves. Dashed lines identify surveys; solid lines identify fisheries."}
local({
  curves <- sim_cod_truth$selectivity
  components <- c("Trawl", "Longline", "Gillnet", "RV", "Sentinel")
  colors <- tam_cols()[c(1, 2, 3, 6, 7)]
  line_types <- c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2)
  plot(range(curves$length), c(0, 1), type = "n",
    xlab = "Length (cm)", ylab = "Selectivity")
  for (i in seq_along(components)) {
    d <- curves[curves$component == components[i], ]
    lines(d$length, d$selectivity, col = colors[i], lty = line_types[i], lwd = 2)
  }
  legend("bottomright", legend = components, col = colors, lty = line_types,
    lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
})
```

`factor(year)` supplies a separate annual scale within each fleet. The
double-logistic curve is its raw four-parameter product; its accompanying scale
is not automatically maximum F. Simpler age groups and penalized smooths are
also available. See [scopes](../reference/for_fleet.html),
[curves](../reference/catchability_curves.html) and
[smooths](../reference/smooth_formulas.html) when extending the example.

## Give surveys their own relationships

```{r survey-formula, cache=TRUE}
dat$index$q_age_group <- cut(dat$index$age, c(0, 3, 5, 7, 9, Inf))
catchability <- ~ 0 +
  for_survey("RV", ~ q_age_group) +
  for_survey("Sentinel", ~ q_age_group)
```

These components estimate separate age-group catchabilities for each survey.
Groups are defined from ages alone, without using simulation truth. Initial
logistic RV and double-logistic Sentinel q fits had weakly identified curve
parameters and failed Hessian checks; the grouped relationship is a different
teaching hypothesis, with those attempts retained. Curves and smooths remain
available when the data support them.

Under the default log link,
q is positive and need not be below one: it relates the supplied index scale to
modeled abundance. A regional survey measures abundance inside its footprint.
Spatial redistribution can change the fraction of the population there, even
when its gear selectivity stays constant. A constant-q relationship to total
abundance is therefore an assumption to inspect, not a consequence of using a
standardized sampling design.
In this realization, the annual fraction of gear-selected fish inside the
footprint ranges from 52–99% for RV and 5–87% for Sentinel. A constant q cannot
fully describe that variation.

## Fit and compare a second hypothesis

```{r separable, cache=TRUE, dependson=c("fleet-formula", "survey-formula"), results='hide'}
separable <- fit_tam(
  dat, ages = 1:14,
  N_settings = list(process = "iid", init = "exp"),
  rec_settings = list(process = "rw"),
  F_settings = list(process = "off", mu_form = fishing, mean_ages = 5:10),
  M_settings = list(process = "off", mu_supplied = ~ I(0.3), mean_ages = 5:10),
  catch_settings = list(sd_form = ~ fleet),
  index_settings = list(q_form = catchability, sd_form = ~ survey)
)
```

For the alternative, replace the free annual scales with AR1 departures around
each fleet's mean age curve:

```{r flexible, cache=TRUE, dependson="separable", results='hide'}
fishing_process <- ~ 0 +
  for_fleet("Trawl", ~ logistic(age)) +
  for_fleet("Longline", ~ logistic(age)) +
  for_fleet("Gillnet", ~ double_logistic(age))

flexible <- update(separable,
  F_settings = list(process = "ar1", mu_form = fishing_process,
                   sd_form = ~ fleet)
)
```

```{r checks}
check_tam(separable, flexible)
```

Age 14 is the modeled plus group, using retained biological inputs through age
20. Average F and M are reported over ages 5–10. The finite-age generator and
the fitted plus group remain an approximation; the dataset records tail losses.

With F process off, each fleet's F follows its formula exactly and has no latent
F process. The alternative does not also estimate an unrestricted annual mean
for its AR1 departures. Process densities operate
separately within fleets; shared correlation parameters do not correlate
innovations between fleets. Observation SD formulas give each fleet and each
survey its own precision.

Both models allow IID cohort-survival variation while holding M at a working
value of 0.3. Those deviations can accommodate departures from assumed mortality;
they do not identify natural mortality separately from other apparent losses.
The generator partitions a pre-generated total mortality budget, so neither
example is its exact generating model. Remaining mortality varies, and regional
availability changes. Parameter uncertainty also conditions on supplied biology.
Inspect numerical and statistical diagnostics before interpreting the extra
process variation.

The shared population experiences total fishing mortality,

\[
F^{\mathrm{total}}_{t,a}=\sum_f F_{t,a,f},
\qquad Z_{t,a}=M_{t,a}+F^{\mathrm{total}}_{t,a}.
\]

Each fleet's catch prediction uses its own F in the Baranov equation, with this
common Z. Catch weights determine yield; stock weights determine biomass and
SSB. Optional typed fleet catch weights must be complete, while stock rows have
no fleet label. Both weight types use kg; the catch-number scale determines
the resulting biomass units.

## Inspect fleets, surveys and the common population

```{r dashboard, eval=FALSE}
vis_tam(Separable = separable, Flexible = flexible, open_file = FALSE)
```

In **Fisheries**, inspect each fleet's yield, catch-at-age, F and residuals;
**Aggregate fishery** follows the fleet pages. The aggregate yield does not create
an aggregate standardized residual. In **Surveys**, check the RV-like and
Sentinel-like fits separately. Inspect age patterns and regional-survey residuals
before interpreting total-population trends.

```{r quantities}
ssb <- get_ssb(Separable = separable, Flexible = flexible)
plot_trend(ssb, color = ~model, colors = tam_pal(2), ylab = "SSB (tonnes)",
           add_buttons = FALSE) |>
  plotly::add_lines(data = sim_cod_truth$annual, x = ~year, y = ~SSB,
    inherit = FALSE, name = "Generating SSB",
    line = list(color = "#333333", dash = "dot"),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}<br>%{y} tonnes<extra>Generating SSB</extra>") |>
  add_plot_buttons()
plot_matrix(get_f(flexible))
```

The dotted SSB line is known generating biomass and has no confidence interval.
Both fitted examples underestimate SSB in this realization despite passing
numerical checks; convergence alone does not establish biological accuracy.
`get_f()` returns total age-specific F. Fleet-specific F is available in
`tidy_pop(flexible)$F_fleet`. The separate simulation truth permits checks of
abundance, mortality and regional availability. Use it to evaluate the fitted
results while keeping it separate from the fitting inputs. This single
realization demonstrates the workflow. It does not establish estimator bias,
interval coverage or which model generalizes best.
